summary: NTP version 4 lets packets carry optional extension fields after the standard header, for capabilities the basic header cannot convey. This standards-track RFC clarifies several points about how those fields are formatted and how they interact with Message Authentication Codes (MACs). It updates RFC 5905, the core NTPv4 specification.

plainLanguage.summary: NTP time messages can carry extra pieces of information after the normal header, for features the header itself cannot express. This RFC sorts out where those extra pieces go, when a message has to be signed, and what a host should do with a piece it does not recognize.

subtitle: Clarifies where optional NTP extension fields go, how they pair with a MAC, and what hosts do with fields they do not know.

tldr.problem: NTPv4 allows optional extension fields and an optional Message Authentication Code, but the text that defines them was wrong: it said a MAC is always present whenever an extension field is, and it left the maximum field size undecided.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC rewrites Section 7.5 of RFC 5905. Extension fields come after the header and before the MAC when one is present, unknown field types are ignored, and new length and algorithm rules cover every combination of fields and MACs.
tldr.outcome: Implementations now have precise rules for reading packets that carry extension fields. The RFC is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 5905 and is itself updated by RFC 9748.

facts.label: Padding
facts.value: Zero-padded to a four-octet word boundary

today: RFC 7822 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2016. It updates RFC 5905, the NTPv4 specification, and is itself updated by RFC 9748. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Why Extension Fields Needed Clarifying
sections.content:
Network Time Protocol version 4 (NTPv4) sends a fixed set of header fields that may be followed by optional fields. There are two kinds of optional field. A Message Authentication Code (MAC) sits at the end of the packet, and it can be 24 octets long, 20 octets long, or a 4-octet crypto-NAK. Extension fields carry capabilities or extra information that the standard header cannot express.

Extension fields were introduced in RFC 5905 as a general mechanism for adding future features without changing the NTP header format. Only two are defined so far: the one used by the Autokey protocol in RFC 5906, and the Checksum Complement of RFC 7821. The Autokey field is always followed by a MAC, and Section 10 of the Autokey specification gives the parsing rules that let a host tell an extension field from a MAC. A MAC is nevertheless not mandatory after an extension field, and an NTPv4 packet may carry one or more extension fields with no MAC at all.

This RFC updates Section 7.5 of RFC 5905 to correct the errors that appeared after that specification was published: the relationship between extension fields and MACs, and the behaviour of a host that receives an extension field it does not know.
sections.plainLanguage: NTP time messages can carry extra pieces of information after the normal header. This RFC sorts out exactly where those extra pieces go and when a message has to be signed.

sections.title: The Extension Field Format
sections.content:
An extension field is a small block made of four parts: a 16-bit Field Type, a 16-bit Length, a Value and Padding. The Field Type says what the field is for, and its value comes from an IANA registry. The Length, Value and Padding contents are defined by the document that the registry entry points to. The Length field is a 16-bit unsigned integer that gives the length of the whole extension field in octets, padding included.

Every extension field is zero-padded to a word, which is four octets, boundary. A field that carries the required fields needs a minimum length of four words, or 16 octets. No field can be longer than 65,532 octets, because the Length field has to be able to hold the size of the field it describes.
sections.plainLanguage: Each extra piece starts with a type number and a length, then holds some data, and is padded with zeros to a four-byte boundary. It must be at least 16 bytes long and cannot be longer than 65,532 bytes.

sections.title: Unknown Field Types
sections.content: Extension fields exist so that new features can be added later, which means a host will meet field types it does not understand. The updated text states that a host that receives an extension field with an unknown Field Type SHOULD ignore that extension field, and MAY drop the packet altogether if policy requires it. Ignoring the unknown field is what allows a new extension to be put into use before every host on the network understands it.
sections.plainLanguage: If a host meets an extension field it does not recognize, it should skip that field. It may also throw the whole packet away if its own policy says so.

sections.title: Extension Fields and Message Authentication Codes
sections.content:
An extension field can travel in a packet that also carries a MAC, for example the one used by Autokey. A specification that defines a new extension field must say whether that field requires a MAC, and if it does, it must define the algorithm used to create the MAC and the length of the MAC that is created. A field may allow more than one algorithm, and in that case the field itself must carry the information about which algorithm was used.

When several extension fields in one packet require a MAC, they must all require the same algorithm and the same MAC length, and a packet must not be sent with two or more such fields that use different algorithms. A receiver that gets two or more recognized extension fields requiring different MAC algorithms must discard the packet. Extension fields that do not require a MAC can be included together with fields that do.

The MAC has one further limit. If no extension field is present, a MAC must not be longer than 24 octets, unless a longer MAC has been agreed between the client and the server. The two can agree on it in an earlier exchange of packets that carried an extension field defining the size and algorithm of the MAC that is transmitted in NTP packets.
sections.plainLanguage: A new kind of extension field has to say whether it needs a signature, and if so, which kind and how long. Two signed fields in one message must use the same kind, and a message that breaks that rule is thrown away.

sections.title: Length Rules Without a MAC
sections.content: A MAC is not required after an extension field, and the updated text gives the sizes that a packet without a MAC must use. If the packet includes a single extension field, the length of that extension field must be at least seven words, which is 28 octets. If the packet includes more than one extension field, the length of the last extension field must be at least 28 octets, and the length of each of the other extension fields must be at least 16 octets.
sections.plainLanguage: Without a signature, a message with one extra field needs that field to be at least 28 bytes long. With several, the last one needs 28 bytes and the others need 16.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC points to the general security discussion for time protocols in RFC 7384 and to the NTP discussion in RFC 5905, and then adds its own notes. Denial-of-service attacks on NTP servers work by flooding a server with a high rate of NTP packets. Malicious use of extension fields cannot make such an attack worse, because servers ignore extension fields they do not know and only respond, if they respond at all, with extension fields they do know. Extension fields that arrive in a packet are neither propagated by a server nor included in a response; a server creates its own extension fields if it needs them for a reply. A large number of extension fields should be flagged by a server as a potential attack, and large extension field sizes should also be flagged unless they are expected to be large.

One further rule protects future extensions. Middleboxes such as firewalls must not filter NTP packets based on their extension fields, and should not examine extension fields in the packets at all, because an NTP packet may carry an extension field that the middlebox has not been updated to recognize.
sections.plainLanguage: Extension fields cannot be used to make a flood attack worse, because servers ignore fields they do not know. Firewalls must not drop NTP packets just because of an extension field they do not understand.
